s: Portuguese harbour fort of Old Muscat · later Oman's main prison, now a museum
el: Prison held about 200 inmates at times
te: The fortress at the harbour gate
se: High on the rocks of Old Muscat, this Portuguese fort guarded the harbour, became a prison and is now a museum
sa: فوق صخور مسقط القديمة يقف هذا الحصن البرتغالي الذي حرس الميناء، ثم صار سجنًا، وهو اليوم متحف
desc: Al Jalali stands on the eastern side of Muscat harbour, facing Al Mirani across the bay. The Portuguese sent Captain Belchior Calaça in 1587 to build it on an earlier Omani site, and it was completed with Al Mirani between 1586 and 1588 as Forte de São João. Persian forces captured the forts in 1738 and again in 1743. For much of the 20th century it was Oman's main prison, holding about 200 prisoners at times, until it closed in the 1970s; it was restored in 1983 as a museum of Omani cultural history.
sig: One of the twin forts that defined Muscat's harbour defences from the Portuguese period to the Al Bu Said state.
refs: Wikipedia contributors. Al Jalali Fort. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jalali_Fort (accessed 9 November 2026)
Archnet. Fort al-Jalali. https://next.archnet.org/sites/22191 (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia (gazetteer point on the fort, ≈50 m). Arabic name is the established name. Timeline start uses 1586; the fort remains standing.

s: Portuguese fort on the west side of Muscat harbour · reopened to visitors in 2025
dr: Built by the Portuguese in 1587 on an earlier fortress
te: The fort that watched the Portuguese leave
se: Across the bay from Al Jalali, Al Mirani guarded Muscat until Omani forces took the city from the Portuguese in 1649
sa: في الجهة المقابلة لقلعة الجلالي حرست قلعة الميراني مسقط حتى انتزعها العمانيون من البرتغاليين عام 1649
desc: Al Mirani was built by the Portuguese in 1587 on top of an earlier fortress, on the west side of Muscat harbour opposite Al Jalali. With Al Jalali it was meant to guard the port against Ottoman advances; in 1623 it was the more important of the two and served as the governor's summer residence. Omani forces under Sultan bin Saif took Muscat in 1649, and the Portuguese who fled into the fort surrendered in January 1650. Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi took control of it in 1749; it later served as a military post and prison, and reopened to the public in April 2025.
sig: A key witness to the end of Portuguese rule in Oman and the rise of the Ya'ariba and Al Bu Said states.
disc: Taken by Ahmad bin Said in 1749
refs: Archnet. Fort al-Mirani. https://next.archnet.org/sites/22192 (accessed 9 November 2026)
Wikipedia contributors. Al Jalali Fort (section on Al Mirani). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jalali_Fort (accessed 9 November 2026)

conf: Coordinates from the Archnet site map point (≈50 m).

s: Watchtower fort above Muttrah harbour · Portuguese towers turned Ya'ariba fort
dr: Towers possibly 1507; present form early Ya'ariba period (1624–1742)
se: Two old watchtowers on a ridge above Muttrah grew into a fort that guarded the trading harbour
sa: برجان قديمان للمراقبة على مرتفع فوق مطرح تحوّلا إلى قلعة تحرس الميناء التجاري
desc: Muttrah Fort crowns a ridge overlooking the harbour and coastal settlement of Muttrah. Its watchtowers may date to 1507 and were probably modified by the Portuguese in the late 16th century. The Ya'ariba (1624–1742) likely turned them into a proper fort early in their rule over Muscat and Muttrah. The Royal Oman Police used it in the late 20th century, and in 2018 it opened to visitors as a venue for arts and cultural events.
sig: Shows how Muscat's twin harbours were defended from the Portuguese era into the Ya'ariba period.
refs: Archnet. Matrah Fort. https://www.archnet.org/sites/22207 (accessed 9 November 2026)
Peterson, J.E. (2007). Historical Muscat: An Illustrated Guide and Gazetteer. Leiden: Brill.
conf: Coordinates from the Archnet site map point (≈50 m). Timeline start uses the possible 1507 date for the towers.

s: Inland fort guarding Old Muscat's water supply · named for irrigation
dr: Built mid-17th century; restored in the 1970s
el: About 1 km inland from Old Muscat
te: The fort that guarded the water
se: In Wadi al-Kabir behind Old Muscat, this small fort protected the wells and gardens that kept the city alive
sa: في الوادي الكبير خلف مسقط القديمة حمى هذا الحصن الصغير الآبار والبساتين التي كانت تمد المدينة بالحياة
desc: Fort al-Rawiyah (Qal'at al-Rawiyah) stands in the Tuyan quarter, about 1 km inland along al-Wadi al-Kabir from Old Muscat. It was built in the mid-17th century, attributed to the Portuguese, to protect Muscat's water supply during the advance of Imam Sultan bin Saif al-Ya'rubi; its name refers to irrigation. It was originally three storeys high, with gardens, a cistern and a well. Sultan bin Ahmad renovated it, and the Ministry of National Heritage and Culture restored it in the 1970s; it now stands two storeys high amid modern housing.
sig: A rare surviving link between Muscat's defences and its water supply.
disc: About 1 km inland from Old Muscat
refs: Archnet. Fort al-Rawiyah. https://next.archnet.org/sites/22226 (accessed 9 November 2026)
Peterson, J.E. (2007). Historical Muscat: An Illustrated Guide and Gazetteer. Leiden: Brill, p. 76.
conf: Coordinates from the Archnet site map point (≈50 m). Arabic name is a careful transliteration of Qal'at al-Rawiyah. Timeline start ≈1650.

s: Coastal outcrop of eclogite · Arabian margin rocks subducted beneath the Samail Ophiolite
dr: Peak garnet growth c. 81–77 Ma; Permian protolith 283.8 ± 0.7 Ma
te: Rocks that went down and came back
ta: صخور غاصت في الأعماق ثم عادت
se: On the beach north of As Sifah lie rare eclogites, pieces of Arabia pushed deep under the ocean crust and brought back to the surface
sa: على الشاطئ شمال السيفة تنكشف صخور إكلوجيت نادرة، وهي قطع من حافة الجزيرة العربية دُفعت عميقًا تحت القشرة المحيطية ثم عادت إلى السطح
desc: The As Sifah eclogites crop out on the coast about 1–2 km north of As Sifah village, in the north-east of the Saih Hatat window. They are the structurally lowest, highest-grade rocks beneath the Samail Ophiolite and record continental-margin rocks subducted to peak conditions of about 2.0–2.5 GPa and 550 °C. Zircon cores show a Permian volcanic protolith (283.8 ± 0.7 Ma). Garnet, zircon and rutile dates (about 80.9 to 75.9 Ma) show garnet growth from about 81 to 77 Ma, during subduction beneath the ophiolite.
sig: A key natural laboratory for dating continental subduction and exhumation beneath the Samail Ophiolite.
refs: Garber, J.M., Rioux, M., Searle, M.P., Kylander-Clark, A.R.C., Hacker, B.R., Vervoort, J.D., Warren, C.J. & Smye, A.J. (2021). Dating continental subduction beneath the Samail Ophiolite: garnet, zircon, and rutile petrochronology of the As Sifah eclogites, NE Oman. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 126, e2021JB022715. https://doi.org/10.1029/2021JB022715
conf: Coordinates are sample CWO237 (23°27'30"N, 58°46'48"E) from Garber et al. (2021); the outcrop extends a few hundred metres. Timeline spans the dated metamorphic growth (≈81 to 75.9 Ma).

s: Fishing village reachable only by sea · home of the Kumzari language
te: The village at the end of the sea road
ta: القرية التي لا يصلها إلا البحر
se: Hidden in a cove near the tip of Musandam, Kumzar can only be reached by boat and keeps its own language
sa: في خليج صغير قرب رأس مسندم تختبئ كمزار، فلا يصلها أحد إلا بالقارب، وما زال أهلها يتحدثون لغتهم الخاصة
desc: Kumzar is a fishing village near the northern tip of the Musandam Peninsula, accessible only by boat, with no road to Khasab. It has been inhabited for about 500 years, and early Portuguese maps show a settlement in the area. Its people speak Kumzari, a Southwestern Iranian language influenced by up to 45 languages including Arabic. Many families keep a second house in Khasab and leave Kumzar from May to September because of the summer heat.
sig: A living example of isolated maritime settlement and linguistic heritage at the Strait of Hormuz.
refs: Wikipedia contributors. Kumzar. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumzar (accessed 9 November 2026)
Wikipedia contributors. Kumzari language. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumzari_language (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia (village point, ≈200 m). The 500-year span is an approximate figure from the source.

s: Bronze and Iron Age collective tombs · at least 188 people and thousands of objects
dr: c. 2000–600 BC (LCG-1 mainly Iron Age I–II)
se: Found by chance in 2012 in Dibba, long stone tombs held the remains of nearly 200 people with bronze, soft-stone vessels and beads
sa: اكتُشفت مصادفة عام 2012 في دبا مقابر حجرية طويلة ضمّت رفات نحو 200 شخص مع أوانٍ برونزية وحجرية وخرز
desc: The site lies on the east coast of the Musandam Peninsula at Dibba al-Bayah, overlooking the Gulf of Oman, and was found by accident in 2012 during infrastructure works. Long Collective Grave 1 (LCG-1), about 14 × 3.5 m and lined with limestone blocks, held at least 188 individuals (153 adults and 35 subadults) in secondary deposition. It yielded 9,666 items, with 1,730 more in five external pits, including 241 soft-stone vessels; a second tomb, LCG-2 (23 × 6 m), produced more than 3,000 objects. Use spans the Wadi Suq period (c. 2000–1600 BC) to Iron Age II, with most material from Iron Age I–II.
sig: One of the richest Bronze–Iron Age funerary deposits in south-east Arabia, studied by an Italian–Omani mission since 2013.
refs: Genchi, F. & Tursi, G. (2022). The softstone vessels assemblage from the Long Collective Grave 1 (LCG-1) at Dibbā al-Bayah (Sultanate of Oman): a preliminary assessment. Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy. https://doi.org/10.1111/aae.12209

ISMEO. Italian Archaeological Expedition to the burials site of Daba (Sultanate of Oman). https://www.ismeo.eu/portfolio_page/italian-archaeological-expedition-to-the-burials-site-of-daba-sultanate-of-oman-2/ (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates from Genchi & Tursi (2022): 25°36'38.78"N, 56°15'28.57"E. Object counts differ between sources (ISMEO gives almost 3,600 objects for LCG-1). Timeline ≈2000–600 BC.

s: High plateau below Jabal Harim · hotspot of new plant records for Oman
te: A mountain garden of rare plants
se: High on Musandam's mountains, the As Sayh plateau and Jabal Harim slopes hold plants found nowhere else in Oman
sa: في أعالي جبال مسندم تحتضن هضبة السيح ومنحدرات جبل الحارم نباتات لا توجد في أي مكان آخر من عُمان
desc: As Sayh is a high plateau with old cultivation terraces beneath Jabal Harim, Musandam's highest mountain. A 2020 botanical study reported 60 new or extended plant records for Oman, about one-third of them (21 species) from Musandam, mostly between about 1,135 and 1,620 m on the As Sayh and As Sahosa slopes of Jabal Harim. Records include Piptatherum holciforme on the Sayh plateau at 1,136 m and Vicia monantha at 1,135 m, while Medicago coronata, new for Arabia, was found on disused terraces at 530 m on the Khasab–Jabal Harim road.
sig: Shows that Musandam's cool uplands hold a distinct, Irano-Turanian-influenced flora still being discovered.
refs: Patzelt, A., Al Hatmi, S., Al Hinai, A., Al Qassabi, Z. & Knees, S.G. (2020). Studies in the flora of Arabia: XXXIV. Sixty new records from the Sultanate of Oman. Edinburgh Journal of Botany 77(3), 413–437. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0960428620000086
conf: Coordinates are the Piptatherum holciforme voucher on the Sayh plateau (25°59'32.3"N, 56°12'51.6"E) in Patzelt et al. (2020). About 2.5 km from the existing Jabal Al Harim geosite, but this record covers the plateau flora. No formal designation; t0 uses the 2020 publication.

na: أفران صهر النحاس في وادي الخطوة
s: Chain of ancient copper smelters along a mountain gorge · copper carried to the Sohar coast
p: Undated (regional smelting from the Bronze Age to early Islamic times)
dr: Not dated; regional smelting periods from the 3rd or 2nd millennium BC to shortly after the arrival of Islam
se: Along the gorges of Wadi Khutwah, clay furnaces and heaps of slag show where people once turned rock into copper
sa: على امتداد شعاب وادي الخطوة تكشف بقايا أفران طينية وأكوام خبث أين حوّل الناس الصخر إلى نحاس
desc: Six copper smelting sites (SM1–SM6) lie on both sides of the gorges of Wadi Khutwah, in the foothills of the Hajar Mountains, with a suspected ore-roasting pit upstream near Sultan's Oasis. Each smelter was built a short distance from a falaj or stream and needed clay for bricks, which often bear the makers' finger impressions, plus large amounts of charcoal and ore. SM6 has more slag cores than any other Khutwah smelter, with debris more than a metre deep in places, suggesting several smelting seasons. The copper was probably cast into small ingots and carried by donkey or camel to the Sohar coast.
sig: A compact, well-mapped example of the small-scale copper industry that made the Oman mountains famous as ancient Magan.
ex: ENHG; Experience Oman Al Buraimi guide
disc: Debris over 1 m deep at SM6
refs: Emirates Natural History Group. Copper smelters of Wadi Khutwah. https://enhg.org/resources/articles/copper/smelter/smelter.htm (accessed 9 November 2026)
Ministry of Heritage and Tourism, Oman. Al Buraimi (visitor guide). https://experienceoman.om/media/gzqg2k1w/buraimi-en.pdf (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates are smelter SM1 (24°19'20"N, 56°07'46"E) from the ENHG survey page, an amateur society source. The smelters themselves are not dated; t0/t1 is a broad estimate from the regional periods given (≈3rd millennium BC to ≈AD 700). Region assigned from the official Buraimi guide, which places Al Khatwa village and falaj in Mahdah; Arabic name is a careful transliteration.

s: Square Sasanian fort in the Sohar hinterland · the only securely dated Late Sasanian fort in Arabia
dr: Built early 5th to mid-6th century AD; used into the 7th century
el: 30 × 30 m with walls about 2.65 m thick
te: A Persian fort on the Batinah
se: Thirteen kilometres inland from the sea near Saham, a square stone fort shows that the Sasanian Persians held this coast before Islam
sa: على بعد 13.5 كيلومترًا من البحر قرب صحم يكشف حصن حجري مربع أن الساسانيين سيطروا على هذا الساحل قبل الإسلام
desc: Fulayj lies on the Batinah plain about 30 km south of Sohar and about 13.5 km inland, near Falaj al-Harth, and was found in the 2012 Saham survey. The fort is square, 30 × 30 m, with walls about 2.65 m thick of unshaped stone and lime mortar, four solid U-shaped corner towers and a single 1.62 m-wide eastern entrance. Thirteen AMS dates place construction and main occupation in the early 5th to mid-6th century AD, including a lime kiln dated to about 415–560 AD, with later use about 625–681 AD. Excavations yielded 2,313 sherds.
sig: Direct evidence of Sasanian military control of the Omani coast before the Islamisation of south-east Arabia.
refs: Al-Jahwari, N.S., Kennet, D., Priestman, S. & Sauer, E. (2018). Fulayj: a Late Sasanian fort on the Arabian coast. Antiquity 92(363), 724–741. https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2018.64
Accepted manuscript: https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/1376210 (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates converted from UTM 40R 479290 E, 2663670 N (WGS 84) given in Al-Jahwari et al.; ≈50 m. Timeline ≈AD 415–670. Arabic name is a careful transliteration.

s: Two tidal inlets with extensive mangroves · Key Biodiversity Area for gulls and kingfishers
dr: Key Biodiversity Area (legacy IBA), last assessed 1994
te: The mangrove creeks of Shinas and Liwa
se: Two tidal creeks on the northern Batinah coast are lined with mangroves where rare kingfishers and big gulls gather
sa: خوران على ساحل الباطنة الشمالي تحفّهما أشجار القرم، تجتمع فيهما طيور الرفراف النادرة والنوارس الكبيرة
desc: Khawr Shinas and Khawr Liwa are two tidal inlets on the northern Batinah coast supporting extensive Avicennia mangrove, together covering about 29.1 km² at 0–5 m altitude. A total of 118 bird species has been recorded, with up to 103 roosting Pallas's gulls (Larus ichthyaetus) in winter. The endangered collared kingfisher subspecies Todirhamphus chloris kalbaensis occurs irregularly in the mangrove, and Sykes's warbler (Hippolais rama) probably breeds. Two nature reserves have been proposed, Khawr Shinas (2,100 ha) and Khawr Nabr (2,300 ha), but none is yet established.
sig: Among the largest mangrove creeks of Oman's Batinah coast and a refuge for a mangrove-dependent kingfisher.
refs: KBA Partnership. Khawr Shinas and Khawr Liwa (KBA 8218). World Database of Key Biodiversity Areas. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8218 (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point, between the two khawrs (≈10 km from each). t0 uses the 1994 assessment.

s: About 300 km of sandy beach and creek mouths · wintering waders, gulls and terns
dr: Key Biodiversity Area (legacy IBA), last assessed 1994
te: The long beach of the shorebirds
se: From Seeb to Shinas, Oman's longest sandy beach is a winter home for sanderlings, gulls and terns
sa: من السيب إلى شناص يمتد أطول شاطئ رملي في عُمان، وهو مشتى لطيور الشاطئ المهاجرة والنوارس وخطاف البحر
desc: The Al Batinah coast Key Biodiversity Area covers about 300 km of exposed sandy beach facing the Gulf of Oman, from As Seeb north-west to Shinas, totalling about 59.1 km² at 0–5 m. Khawrs form at the mouths of drainage lines, though most are transitory; five major khawrs (Kalba, Shinas, Liwa, Ra's/Juzor as Sawadi and Al Qurm) are assessed as separate sites. Sanderling (Calidris alba) occurs in important numbers in winter, along with roosting gulls and terns. Seven Nature Conservation Areas totalling 860 ha have been proposed along the coast.
sig: The main sandy-shore habitat for wintering shorebirds on Oman's most populated coast.
refs: KBA Partnership. Al Batinah coast (KBA 8220). World Database of Key Biodiversity Areas. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8220 (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point for a linear site about 300 km long, so the pin is only a representative point. t0 uses the 1994 assessment.

s: Fort built over a rock outcrop at the foot of Jebel Nakhal · pre-Islamic origins, 1834 towers
dr: Pre-Islamic origins; rebuilt 17th century; extended 1834; restored 1990
el: Six towers on a rocky outcrop
te: The fort that grew out of the rock
se: Nakhal Fort rises straight out of a rocky hill, its walls wrapped around the natural stone above the palm groves
sa: ترتفع قلعة نخل مباشرة من تل صخري، وتلتف جدرانها حول الحجر الطبيعي فوق بساتين النخيل
desc: Nakhal Fort sits on a rocky prominence at the foot of Jebel Nakhal, overlooking palm groves and the route to the Ain al-Thawarah spring, about 120 km west of Muscat. Its origins are believed to be pre-Islamic, and it was rebuilt in the 17th century under the Bani Kharous and Ya'ariba imams. The gateway and towers seen today were extensions of 1834 attributed to Said bin Sultan. Six towers encircle the two-storey fort, which incorporates the natural rock into its structure; the last major restoration was in 1990.
sig: A classic example of an Omani fort shaped by and built into its rock foundation.
refs: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism, Oman. Nakhl Fort. https://experienceoman.om/destinations/al-batinah-south/nakhl-fort (accessed 9 November 2026)
Wikipedia contributors. Nakhal Fort. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakhal_Fort (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia, matching the official Experience Oman map box (centre ≈23.3947 N, 57.8289 E); ≈100 m. Timeline start ≈AD 600 for the pre-Islamic origin is an estimate.

s: Fortress-palace of Imam Sultan bin Saif II · stone vaults with no wood
el: Ceilings of stone vaults, with no timber
se: Built in 1708 for an imam, Al Hazm has stone-vaulted ceilings, secret passages and old Portuguese and Spanish cannons
sa: بُنيت قلعة الحزم عام 1708 لإمام عُماني، وفيها أسقف حجرية مقببة وممرات سرية ومدافع برتغالية وإسبانية قديمة
desc: Al Hazm Castle stands on flat land beside Wadi Rustaq in Al Batinah South. It was built in 1120 AH / 1708 AD by Imam Sultan bin Saif II as his residence, and he was buried within it after his death in 1718. The square castle has two towers reached by stairways designed for horses, two gateways, and ceilings carried on stone arches without wood. It houses Portuguese and Spanish cannons, tunnels and secret passages, and rooms once used for teaching the Qur'an and sciences; it was restored in 1996.
sig: A late Ya'ariba fortress-palace that shows the peak of Omani defensive architecture.
refs: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism, Oman. Al Hazm Castle. https://experienceoman.om/destinations/al-batinah-south/al-hazm-castle (accessed 9 November 2026)
Wikipedia contributors. Al Hazm Castle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hazm_Castle (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia, matching the official Experience Oman map box (centre ≈23.5507 N, 57.4728 E); ≈50 m.

na: موقع التيخة من فترة أم النار
s: Large Early Bronze Age settlement with round towers near Rustaq
el: About 50 ha, 35 ha with Umm an-Nar occupation
te: A Bronze Age village of towers
se: On a terrace of Wadi Far near Rustaq, people of the Umm an-Nar age built round towers, houses and stone tombs
sa: على مصطبة في وادي الفرع قرب الرستاق بنى أهل فترة أم النار أبراجًا دائرية وبيوتًا ومقابر حجرية
desc: Al-Tikha lies about 5 km north of old Rustaq on a Quaternary alluvial terrace on the west bank of Wadi Far, just south of its confluence with Wadi Sahtan. The site covers about 50 ha, with about 35 ha of Umm an-Nar occupation, including three certain round towers. Occupation area S1 has about 20 stone structures on roughly 1 ha, and S2 is a courtyard complex of about 1,000 m². The cemetery has at least four tombs and is tentatively dated from 2700–2600 BC, reaching its greatest extent in 2600–2200 BC; a transect survey collected about 3,500 sherds.
sig: One of the largest documented Umm an-Nar settlements on the Batinah side of the Hajar Mountains, informing how third-millennium communities lived.
refs: Deadman, W.M., Kennet, D., de Vreeze, M. & al-Jahwari, N.S. (2022). The nature of third-millennium settlement: the example of al-Tikha (Rustaq), an Umm an-Nar site on the Batinah coast of Oman. Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 33, 49–84. https://doi.org/10.1111/aae.12218
conf: Coordinates converted from UTM 40N ≈544200 E, 2592100 N (WGS 84) printed in Deadman et al. (2022; northing misprinted there as 25921001), ≈100 m. Chronology is described by the authors as tentative. Arabic name is a careful transliteration.

n: Ra's as Sawadi and Juzor as Sawadi
s: Headland, khawr and eight islands · breeding herons, ospreys and sooty falcons
dr: Key Biodiversity Area (legacy IBA), last assessed 1994; proposed National Scenic Reserve
el: About 10.1 km²; c. 25 pairs of Western Reef Heron
te: The islands of the reef herons
se: Off the Sawadi headland, eight small islands shelter nesting herons, ospreys and sooty falcons above coral reefs
sa: قبالة رأس السوادي تأوي ثماني جزر صغيرة أعشاش البلشون والعقاب النساري وصقر الغروب فوق شعاب مرجانية
desc: Ra's as Sawadi is a headland north-west of As Seeb with a khawr, beach, sandbars and eight offshore islands, covering about 10.1 km² at 0–30 m. About 25 pairs of Western Reef Heron (Egretta gularis) and at least two pairs of Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) breed on the islands, which are also an important breeding site for Sooty Falcon (Falco concolor). Extensive mudflats in the khawr hold wintering and passage waterbirds, and high-quality coral reefs surround the islands. The two largest islands hold settlement sites more than 4,000 years old.
sig: A compact mix of seabird islands, coral and mudflat on the Batinah coast, still only proposed for protection.
refs: KBA Partnership. Ra's as Sawadi - Juzor as Sawadi (KBA 8222). World Database of Key Biodiversity Areas. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8222 (accessed 9 November 2026)
conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point (≈2 km). t0 uses the 1994 assessment.

s: Walled clifftop quarter guarding Ibri oasis · towers, souq and falaj
dr: More than 600 years old (visitor guide); documented 2012–2013
el: Seven towers on a rocky cliff
te: The fortress village on the cliff
se: On a rocky cliff at the edge of Ibri oasis, the walled mud-brick town of Al Sulaif has towers, a souq and a falaj running beneath it
sa: على جرف صخري عند طرف واحة عبري تقف بلدة السليف المسوّرة المبنية من الطين، بأبراجها وسوقها وفلجها الذي يجري تحتها
desc: Harat as-Sulayf is a walled settlement on a rocky cliff at the eastern edge of the Ibri oasis, controlling access to the oasis. Mud-brick buildings on stone foundations, mostly two storeys, line streets running up and down the slope, with a mosque, a souq and access points to an underground falaj. The castle is said to be more than 600 years old and has seven towers and extensive battlements, with Quranic quotations and hand imprints on some arches. The site was documented in 2012–2013 for a heritage management and development plan for the Ministry of Heritage and Culture.
sig: A well-preserved fortified oasis quarter showing how settlements, defence and water were integrated in Ad Dhahirah.
